drills.q: True or false: the safest way to rotate a secret is to revoke the old credential immediately after generating the new one, minimizing the exposure window.
drills.a: False -- revoking immediately, before every reader has picked up the new credential, causes an outage for any reader still using the old one. The grace period must exceed the slowest reader's refresh cadence.

drills.q: What's the 2026 consensus TTL range for a JWT access token, and why not just use 1 hour?
drills.a: 5-15 minutes. A 1-hour TTL means a compromised or should-be-revoked token stays dangerous for up to an hour with no additional infrastructure needed to bound that -- the TTL is a direct blast-radius cap.

drills.q: Why can't a legacy application with a hardcoded database connection string use Vault dynamic secrets as-is?
drills.a: Dynamic secrets require the application to be lease-aware -- able to request/renew a fresh credential before the lease's TTL expires. A hardcoded connection string read once at startup has no such renewal mechanism.

drills.q: A rotation script generates a new DB credential, immediately drops the old DB user, then updates the config store. Half the fleet starts throwing auth errors. Diagnose.
drills.a: The old credential was revoked before the grace period allowed slower readers (cached config, infrequent restarts) to pick up the new one -- classic dual-secret pattern violation. Fix: create new, wait for a grace period exceeding the slowest reader's refresh cadence, THEN revoke old.

drills.q: Explain why refresh token rotation with reuse detection makes a 30-day refresh token acceptably safe despite being long-lived.
drills.a: Every refresh token is single-use; using it invalidates itself and issues a new one. A stolen refresh token, once the legitimate client has rotated past it, becomes detectable the moment it's replayed -- the replay of an already-invalidated token is the theft signal, triggering revocation of the entire token family.

drills.q: A team adds a Redis-backed JWT deny list and reports request latency increased noticeably across the whole API. What's the likely mistake, and the fix?
drills.a: The deny-list lookup is being hit on every single request with no local caching. Fix: cache the 'not revoked' result locally with a short TTL (seconds), chosen against the actual revocation-propagation SLA needed, instead of hitting Redis on every request.

drills.q: An admin clicks 'revoke user session' in a pure short-TTL JWT system with no deny list. How long can the user realistically keep acting, and why?
drills.a: Up to the full remaining lifetime of their most recently issued access token (5-15 min TTL) -- the refresh token is invalidated immediately so no new access tokens can be minted, but an already-issued access token has no revocation mechanism and remains valid until its own exp.

drills.q: Design the rotation for a shared database credential used by 50 service instances with varying config-cache TTLs (some 1 minute, some 30 minutes) and a weekly deploy cadence for the slowest consumer. What determines the grace period?
drills.a: The grace period must exceed the SLOWEST reader's actual refresh mechanism -- here, that's whichever is longer between the 30-minute cache TTL and the weekly deploy cadence for any consumer that only re-reads config on restart/deploy. If any consumer only refreshes on deploy, the grace period effectively needs to span up to that deploy cadence, not just the longest cache TTL.

drills.q: Why does a Secrets Manager rotation Lambda demote the old credential to AWSPREVIOUS instead of deleting it in the finishSecret step, and what's the tradeoff of retaining it indefinitely?
drills.a: Retaining it as AWSPREVIOUS provides an immediate rollback path if the newly-promoted credential has a problem discovered shortly after rotation. The tradeoff: retaining it indefinitely leaves a valid-but-unused credential as its own lingering exposure -- teams should set an explicit retention/cleanup policy rather than leaving AWSPREVIOUS unmanaged forever.

drills.q: A fleet of 50 microservices shares a handful of databases; 40 are legacy with hardcoded connection strings, 10 are newer and cloud-native. Design the secrets strategy.
drills.a: Mixed approach: adopt Vault dynamic secrets for the 10 lease-aware-capable services (centralizes issuance/expiry/revocation, better amortized operational cost at scale), and keep disciplined static-secret dual-secret rotation for the 40 legacy services rather than forcing a refactor or forcing dynamic secrets onto apps that can't handle mid-operation lease expiry gracefully.

drills.q: A team claims caching JWT signature-verification results is equivalent in value to caching a Redis deny-list lookup. Evaluate and correct this claim.
drills.a: Not equivalent -- signature verification is a local cryptographic operation with no network call and negligible cost; caching it saves little and risks incorrectly treating a token as valid past a boundary if done wrong. Deny-list lookup caching avoids a real network round-trip to Redis on every request, a genuinely meaningful cost -- the two are different classes of optimization.
